raw_response:
I've been farming this land since I was maybe fifteen years old, helping my father. I know this land. I know what works here. Quzhou soil is decent — loam, good for wheat and corn. My father grew wheat and corn, my neighbors grow wheat and corn, and I grow wheat and corn. That's how it is here.

I have about 12 mu. I'll put 10 mu into the winter wheat now, then after the June harvest I'll turn that same ground over to summer maize. That's the only rotation that makes sense here — two crops on the same land, same family has done it this way forever.

Maybe 2 mu I'll keep for vegetables behind the house — garlic, beans, cabbage — for the family to eat. That's not really a cash crop, so I won't count it in the plan.

For wheat seeds I'll buy what the village seed shop has — Kenong 199 is what most people around here use now. For maize I'll buy Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed. The hybrid costs a bit more but the yield is better. I've used it three years running.

Fertilizer — I buy compound fertilizer in bags and spread it at planting, then add urea when the wheat starts jointing in spring. More fertilizer means more grain. I don't want to risk a thin harvest. Same for maize — I put down compound at seeding and urea when the plant is knee-high.

Water is the worry. Hebei is dry. I'll pump groundwater three times for wheat — once before sowing if the soil is dry, once in March at jointing, once when the heads are forming. For maize the summer rains help, but I'll pump at least twice to be safe.

Pests — I spray for aphids on wheat in May, and maybe once more if I see disease. Maize I usually only spray once, maybe not at all if the year is good.

Tillage — I hire a rotary tiller from the village cooperative before I plant wheat in October. For maize after wheat harvest I rotary till again to break up the stubble.
